description: Captures cases where the source code defines functional input parameters, optional flags, or enumeration options that are omitted entirely from the natural-language description. For example, code signatures may contain pagination limits, format flags, or authorization tokens that callers must supply but the text documentation never mentions.

Captures instances where the code signature or parameter processing directly conflicts with what the description documents, such as claiming a parameter is user-configurable when it is hardcoded in the body. For example, a description might instruct callers to supply a unit string or bracket code, while the implementation expects raw numeric values or completely ignores the parameter.

Captures implicit input constraints enforced in code that restrict execution boundaries, such as mandatory numerical ranges, character caps, formatting rules, or array length limits. For example, the code might silently clamp pagination inputs between specific lower and upper bounds or enforce regex pattern checks on identifier strings.

Captures situations where the underlying source code does not perform the primary action promised by the description, such as throwing an unimplemented error, returning mock data, or executing a different operation altogether. For example, a tool described as extracting document text or calculating multiple metrics might raise an unhandled exception or return only a single value.

Captures discrepancies where the actual output fields, data types, or return shapes generated by the code differ from or enrich what the description communicates. For example, the code might return a multi-key dictionary containing status codes, counts, and calculated metadata when the text implies a simple scalar value or plain string.

Captures hidden operational requirements in the implementation, such as mandatory environment variables, active session contexts, background service connections, or external approval gates. For example, execution may depend on required API authorization tokens or active database connections that the text documentation leaves completely unmentioned.

Captures internal exception handling logic, safety checks, or fallback routines in the code that manage edge cases without surfacing them in the description. For example, the code might silently fall back to default values when invalid inputs are passed, or return specific error payloads when requested resources are missing.

Captures underlying data processing mechanics present in the implementation—such as case-insensitive search, accent stripping, string normalization, or multi-field sorting logic—that alter query results. For example, code might perform substring matching across multiple attributes or normalize entity names before executing a lookup without documenting these search behaviors.
